slides.title: Handling your first Zillow lead
slides.lead: Day 2 · 90 minutes including discussion and practice
slides.body:
Know what you received.
Know how to begin.

Learn how to respond to the lead, lead the first conversation, and agree on a useful next step with the buyer.
slides.theme: tru alms alms-cover training-depth
slides.notes:
Introduce yourself. Day 1 covered the record; today teaches the conversation and the actions that belong in that record. Ask participants to open their learner session for submissions.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, INT-016. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.title: A live connection puts a buyer on the phone
slides.lead: Zillow calls you first. You review the inquiry, then connect to the waiting buyer.
slides.body:
Answer the incoming call. Zillow provides information about the buyer and the home before you speak to the buyer.

Read the inquiry, then connect. In this example, the buyer asks about a property’s HOA fee. Begin by introducing yourself and acknowledging that question.

Source: Zillow Conversion Playbook, page 7. Zillow’s published demonstration; screens vary by app version.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson training-depth
slides.notes:
Point to Accept on the first screen and Connect on the second. These are Zillow’s own simulated training screens. Read the inquiry. The names and address belong to Zillow’s illustration, not our later practice case. The current In-App Connections FAQ confirms answer/review/connect. Do not read every property field.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, INT-012; Zillow Conversion Playbook Oct 2023 p7; Zillow In-App Connections FAQ Oct 2025. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.title: Real-Time Touring asks you to accept a tour
slides.lead: The phone alert identifies Real-Time Touring. The app then shows the buyer’s requested times.
slides.body:
Review the request in the app. Zillow gives you five minutes to accept a time you can attend or pass on the request.

This is not a live buyer transfer. After accepting, review the booking details and contact the buyer about the appointment.

Source: Zillow Real-Time Touring demonstration. Zillow’s published demonstration; screens vary by app version.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson training-depth
slides.notes:
Read the Real-Time Touring label and buyer-selected times. Distinguish Zillow’s five-minute acceptance window from the five-minute first-contact standard taught here. Dates and property are sample data. Eric’s “not a live call” means no live buyer conversation; do not teach that the phone never rings. Booking uses ShowingTime availability. Follow actual status and notifications.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, INT-012; Zillow Real-Time Touring page and linked Oct 2025 demonstration. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.title: A standard tour request tells you what the buyer wants
slides.lead: The buyer has asked to see a particular home. They may have supplied a preferred day and time.
slides.body:
Read the request before you contact them. Use the property and preferred time in your opening so the buyer does not have to start over.

“I see you requested a tour Saturday afternoon. Would that still work for you? I’ll check the showing arrangements and confirm the details.”

A standard tour request may arrive as a live connection or an alert in Follow Up Boss. If the buyer is not already on the phone, your next job is to contact them.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson lesson-photo photo-home training-depth
slides.notes:
Explain Follow Up Boss in full before abbreviating it to FUB. Show how the request gives you an opening. Distinguish preferred timing from booking status without making that obvious distinction into a quiz.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, INT-012. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.title: Give your best guess: how quickly should you call?
slides.lead: A 2007 study of web leads found 100 times higher odds of making contact when the first call happened within ___ rather than 30 minutes. Which timeframe fills the blank? Choose an answer, then explain why.
slides.body:
Source: InsideSales.com / James Oldroyd, 2007 Lead Response Management Study. Historical web-lead research.

Compare with the teaching example

Within 5 minutes. The study compared calls at five minutes with calls at 30 minutes and reported 100 times higher odds of contact. It studied web leads across six companies, not Zillow buyers specifically. The practical point: respond while the request is fresh.

This is a prediction to start the discussion, not a test of a rule you have already learned. Ask what may change for a buyer while they wait. The research measured time from the web inquiry; our training standard starts when the agent receives the lead.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson alms-exercise training-depth lesson-question
slides.notes:
Ask for a choice and a reason. People without HQ access can answer aloud; select an option on your presenter slide to discuss it. Learners with access submit their own choice and explanation. Say: “Give me your best guess. Then tell me why you think timing would matter.” Hear a few answers before revealing five minutes. Attribute the statistic to the 2007 InsideSales.com and James Oldroyd study, not Zillow. Do not describe higher odds as a guaranteed result for an individual buyer.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, INT-016. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.title: Call promptly when the buyer has asked to hear from you
slides.lead: For a new lead received during normal business hours, 8 a.m.–8 p.m., call within five minutes unless the buyer gave a different contact instruction.
slides.body:
The buyer just asked for help with a home. A call lets you hear their tone, answer questions as they arise, and begin a conversation about what they need.

Follow Up Boss may already have sent an automated introduction. That does not replace your own call. If the buyer requested a later callback or asked for text, respect that instruction.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson lesson-photo photo-follow-up training-depth
slides.notes:
Explain Eric’s reason: the buyer just expressed interest, rather than being a random person being interrupted. Hearing and responding in real time matters. Do not repeat unverified response-rate statistics. The clock starts at agent receipt; do not invent after-hours rules.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, INT-009, INT-011–013. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.title: If the call goes unanswered, send a personal text
slides.lead: Example: a buyer requested a tour of 418 Cedar Lane. You just called, but they did not answer. The address is fictional.
slides.body:
“Hi, this is [your name] with [your brokerage]. I just tried calling about your Zillow request to see 418 Cedar Lane. I’d be happy to help arrange a tour. I’m available for a call at 4 or 6 today. Would either time work for you?”

Tell them who called, connect the call to their request, and offer a clear opportunity to talk. Use times you can actually make. You are offering a phone call here, not confirming a tour.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson training-depth
slides.notes:
Read the example with your own name and brokerage. Distinguish phone-call availability from tour availability. This personal text follows the missed call. Next, explain how this first attempt fits into the ongoing outreach plan.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, INT-011. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.
Handoff: Next: Keep working a new lead that has not answered. Connect it to the action you just practiced.
slides.cue: Next: Keep working a new lead that has not answered. Connect it to the action you just practiced.

slides.title: Keep working a new lead that has not answered
slides.lead: The first missed call and personal text are the beginning of your outreach, not the entire plan.
slides.body:
Day one: Aim for three to four personal touches, with at least two calls and one personal text in the normal unanswered-lead flow.

First week: Aim for ten total touches, including day one. Make most attempts calls, vary the contact times, and make each text relevant to the inquiry.

Once the buyer responds: Follow the conversation and the plan you agree together. The unanswered-lead quota no longer applies. Honor stated contact restrictions throughout.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson lesson-timeline training-depth
slides.notes:
These are the newer September 12 standards. Automation is not personal effort. Do not invent a compressed late-day schedule or a quota for an engaged buyer. Explain why repeating “just checking in” is not useful persistence.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, INT-027–029, INT-054; R019. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.title: Respond to a buyer who is at work
slides.lead: A new Zillow inquiry arrives at 2 p.m. The buyer writes: “I’m at work. Please call at 5 about the Cedar Lane home.” What should you do next? Choose an answer, then explain why.
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

“Hi, I’m [your name] with [your brokerage]. I’ll be the agent calling at 5 about the Cedar Lane home. If you have questions before then, you’re welcome to text me.” Call at 5 as requested.

Acknowledge now so the buyer knows who will call. The requested time governs the call; the default does not justify interrupting them at work.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson alms-exercise training-depth lesson-question
slides.notes:
Ask for a choice and a reason. People without HQ access can answer aloud; select an option on your presenter slide to discuss it. Learners with access submit their own choice and explanation. Hear the responses first, then reinforce Eric’s exception: acknowledge by text now and call at the requested time. Demonstrate “I’ll be the agent calling you at five.” Then let learners choose and explain. Review whether it introduces the agent and preserves the callback. Earlier availability is optional.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, INT-016. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.title: Use LEAD to guide the conversation
slides.lead: Introduce yourself. Ask for the appointment. Learn what matters. Confirm the plan.
slides.body:
1. L — Lead with who you are: Introduce yourself: your name, brokerage, connection to Zillow, and why you’re calling.
  2. E — Extend the invitation: Immediately after your introduction, ask for the appointment. Offer the buyer two concrete times to meet with you.
  3. A — Ask questions that move the conversation forward: Ask where they want to live, what prompted their search, and what matters to them. Use their answers to ask the next useful question.
  4. D — Deliver the summary: Summarize what matters to the buyer, confirm the next steps, and build momentum toward the appointment.

You may also know Zillow’s ALMS: Appointment, Location, Motivation, Summarize. LEAD includes your introduction and uses location and motivation to guide your questions.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson lesson-framework training-depth
slides.notes:
After introducing yourself, ask for the appointment and offer two concrete times. Then ask questions that move the conversation forward: where they want to live, what prompted their search, and what matters. Use each answer to choose the next useful question. Summarize next steps to build momentum into the appointment.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, INT-016, INT-021. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.title: Which opening serves the buyer’s request?
slides.lead: A buyer requested a Zillow tour but selected no time. Both agents introduce themselves. Choose the continuation you would use, then explain what the other version could communicate to the buyer.
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

The appointment-first opening helps with the request immediately. Asking about readiness before offering the visit can make the buyer feel they must qualify for help. Discovery still belongs in the call, after the early invitation and permission.

An early invitation belongs here because the buyer asked to see the home. This is about order and purpose, not banning useful questions.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson alms-exercise training-depth lesson-question
slides.notes:
Ask for a choice and a reason. People without HQ access can answer aloud; select an option on your presenter slide to discuss it. Learners with access submit their own choice and explanation. Allow a minute to respond. Ask what the interview-first agent hoped to learn, then show where discovery belongs after the invitation. Do not shame a choice. Demonstrate a revised opening.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, INT-016. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.title: What would you ask about needing more space?
slides.lead: The buyer says, “We need more space, but we don’t want to leave our neighborhood.”
slides.body:
1. What does that tell you?
  2. What do you still need to understand?
After your answer: review the explanation
Ask what the extra space would let them do. Follow the answer: a quiet work area is different from storage or a larger gathering space. Confirm your understanding before treating a feature as a requirement.

fields.label: What would you do, and why? What information would change your answer?

activity.model: Ask what the extra space would let them do. Follow the answer: a quiet work area is different from storage or a larger gathering space. Confirm your understanding before treating a feature as a requirement.

slides.title: Questions you can use to start a conversation
slides.lead: Choose a question that fits what the buyer has already told you. Use the answer to decide what to ask next.
slides.body:
1. What made you click on this particular home?
  2. Have you had a chance to look at other homes in the market?
  3. What other homes have you been considering?
  4. Where are you moving from?
  5. Which areas are you considering, and what draws you to them?
  6. What would you like your next home to do differently?
  7. What prompted you to start looking?
  8. Is this your first home purchase, or have you bought before?
  9. What timing would work best for you?
  10. What have you liked or disliked about the homes you’ve seen?

Go deeper: “Tell me more about that.” · “What makes that important to you?” · “What would that change for you?”
slides.theme: tru alms lesson training-depth
slides.notes:
Give agents a usable menu, not a list they must finish. Read two or three starters and ask a volunteer to answer one. Demonstrate a follow-up based on the answer. For “more space,” ask what they need room for. For an area, ask what makes it work for them. Check that the buyer has time for the conversation. The full question bank is in the reference.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, Eric September 15 refinement; INT-016, INT-021. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.title: Choose the next question you would ask
slides.lead: During a first call, a buyer tells you: “We’re already in town. We need more space, but we don’t want to leave our neighborhood.” Which question would you ask first? Choose an answer, then explain why.
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

“What is feeling too tight in your current home?” This could reveal whether they need bedrooms, work space, storage or something else. Then explore why staying in the neighborhood matters.

A useful question follows the buyer’s words and reveals a reason or tradeoff that shapes the search.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson alms-exercise training-depth lesson-question
slides.notes:
Ask for a choice and a reason. People without HQ access can answer aloud; select an option on your presenter slide to discuss it. Learners with access submit their own choice and explanation. Give a minute to choose, then compare two questions. Ask what a possible answer would tell the agent. Different wording is not an error; look for curiosity tied to the situation.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, INT-016. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.title: Follow the answer before choosing a feature
slides.lead: Fictional conversation after the appointment invitation.
slides.body:
Agent asks

“What would the extra space let you do?”

Buyer explains

“I take work calls at the kitchen table. Everyone has to stay quiet.”

Agent follows up

“Would a separate room solve that, or do you also need distance from the main living area?”

Agent checks

“So being able to close a door and take calls matters more than the total square footage. Have I understood that?”

slides.title: Practice a short discovery conversation
slides.lead: One person plays a buyer who wants to stay in the neighborhood but needs more space. The other plays the agent, after an appointment has been discussed. Choose a conversation starter, then find out what “more space” means.
slides.body:
First turn: 4 minutes. Talk for two minutes, give one minute of specific feedback, then use one minute to retry.

Switch buyer and agent: 4 minutes. Use a different reason for needing space. Everyone practices speaking and listening.

Use one minute to form pairs and two minutes to debrief. Submit your reflection when you return.

Compare with the teaching example

Choose a relevant starter, explore the current situation, and follow the answer. Learning that the buyer works at the kitchen table points toward a work-space need, not automatically more bedrooms.

Record what you actually learned and changed. Reflection does not prove a coach observed the call.

slides.chapter: 4. Work through concerns and agree on the next step
slides.title: Common objections you may hear
slides.lead: Different words can hide very different concerns. Start by understanding what is behind the buyer’s hesitation.
slides.body:
1. “I only had a question about the home.”
  2. “I’m not ready to buy yet.”
  3. “I’m uncertain about the market.”
  4. “I’m worried about the monthly payment.”
  5. “We need to sell our home first.”
  6. “The home I wanted is already under contract.”
  7. “I only want to speak with the listing agent.”
  8. “I don’t want to commit to an agent yet.”

Which have you heard? What did the buyer actually need help understanding?
slides.theme: tru alms lesson training-depth
slides.notes:
Invite two people to name a concern they have heard. Do not diagnose it from the label alone: “not ready” could mean timing, money, uncertainty, or simply wanting information first. You do not need a separate memorized speech for each item.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, Eric September 15 objection framework; INT-016–018. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.title: What would you ask before offering a solution?
slides.lead: The buyer says they are uncertain about the market and hesitate when you offer a visit.
slides.body:
1. What might they mean by “uncertain”?
  2. How would different answers change the help you offer?
After your answer: review the explanation
Ask what part concerns them. A fear of choosing the wrong home calls for different help than uncertainty about payment. Offer an action based on the answer and check whether it would help. Avoid predictions or pressure.

fields.label: What would you do, and why? What information would change your answer?

slides.chapter: 4. Work through concerns and agree on the next step
slides.title: Understand the concern before offering help
slides.lead: Help the buyer work through the concern. Do not rush past it to get back to your script.
slides.body:
1. Acknowledge the concern: Recognize what feels difficult or uncertain. “I hear you—this is a big decision.”
  2. Ask questions to understand: Find out what is underneath it. “What part is worrying you most?” Then follow their answer.
  3. Offer a solution: Propose a specific next step that addresses what you learned. Explain how it helps, then ask, “Would that be useful?”

An objection is not resolved just because you delivered a response. Listen to whether the proposed next step actually helps.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson lesson-framework lesson-three training-depth
slides.notes:
Model empathy without assuming you know the problem. Ask before prescribing. A question about the roof may be about repair costs or a previous bad experience. A market concern may be about timing, payment, or making the wrong choice. The solution should follow the answer. If the buyer declines, respect that and agree on an appropriate next step.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, Eric September 15 objection framework. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.chapter: 4. Work through concerns and agree on the next step
slides.title: “I’m uncertain about the market right now.”
slides.lead: Example: the buyer is interested in the home but hesitates when you offer an appointment. Find out what is behind the concern before offering a solution.
slides.body:
Acknowledge“I hear you. It’s a big decision, and you want to feel comfortable with it.”

Ask“What is worrying you most about buying right now?”

Buyer“I’m worried we’ll rush and choose the wrong home.”

Offer a solution“We can use a visit to learn what works for you and compare it with other options. You don’t have to decide to buy today. Would seeing it with that purpose help?”
slides.theme: tru alms lesson lesson-photo photo-concern training-depth
slides.notes:
Read the buyer’s concern before the response. Emphasize that this buyer is worried about choosing the wrong home; we learned that by asking. Do not use the same solution automatically if the concern is affordability or a need to sell first. Do not predict rates or prices. Explain actual touring agreements accurately if asked; do not promise there are no forms or obligations.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, Eric September 15 objection framework. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.chapter: 4. Work through concerns and agree on the next step
slides.title: A property question may have a concern behind it
slides.lead: A buyer says, “I only wanted to know about the roof. Our last house had an expensive leak, and I’m not ready to schedule anything.” You have not verified the roof information. Which response best acknowledges, explores, and offers relevant help? Choose an answer, then explain why.
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

“After that experience, I understand why the roof matters. What would you want to know before feeling comfortable taking another look? I can verify that information and we can decide on the next step from there.” Then listen. The buyer may need repair records, an answer about age, or help understanding what remains unknown. Do not guess the facts or make the answer conditional on a visit.

The response recognizes the experience, asks what information would help, and offers to verify it. An invitation can follow when it helps with the concern; it should not skip over the concern.
slides.theme: tru alms lesson alms-exercise training-depth lesson-question
slides.notes:
Ask for a choice and a reason. People without HQ access can answer aloud; select an option on your presenter slide to discuss it. Learners with access submit their own choice and explanation. Take a choice and a reason, then ask two volunteers to say their own version using acknowledge, ask, and offer. Compare what each response assumes. Acknowledge does not mean pretending to know how the buyer feels. A useful solution follows the buyer’s answer.

Sources: TRU September 12 teaching, INT-016. Examples are fictional unless credited to Zillow. Use true names, brokerage, availability and property facts.

slides.title: From the next lead to the next step
slides.lead: Today, you practiced the complete first-conversation process. Take these four actions into your next lead.
slides.body:
1. Recognize the lead. Know whether you are joining a live buyer or responding to a new request.
  2. Start the conversation. Respond promptly, introduce yourself, and offer a useful appointment.
  3. Understand the buyer. Follow their answers and work through concerns with empathy, questions, and a solution.
  4. Agree and follow through. Summarize the plan, record it in FUB, and do what you promised.

Keep your conversation starters and practice reference handy ↗

questionBank:
Conversation starters to keep beside you

Choose what fits the conversation. You do not need to ask every question. Start with what the buyer already told you and follow their answers.

Open the conversation

  1. What made you click on this particular home?
  2. Have you had a chance to look at other homes in the market?
  3. What other homes have you been considering?
  4. What have you liked or disliked about the homes you’ve seen?
  5. Is this your first home purchase, or have you bought before?

Understand what matters

  1. Where are you moving from?
  2. Which areas are you considering, and what draws you to them?
  3. What is working well in your current home?
  4. What would you like your next home to do differently?
  5. What prompted you to start looking?
  6. What would that extra space let you do?

Explore timing and decisions

  1. What timing would work best for you?
  2. What needs to happen before you can make a move?
  3. Who else would you like involved in looking at homes or making the decision?

Follow an answer

  1. Tell me more about that.
  2. What makes that important to you?
  3. What would that change for you?
  4. What would help you feel comfortable with the next step?

When a buyer raises a concern

  1. Acknowledge the concern: recognize the worry or frustration before moving on.
  2. Ask questions to understand: What part concerns you most? What happened before? What would you need to know?
  3. Offer a solution: propose a specific action tied to their answer, then check whether it would help.

Useful next steps may include verifying property information, comparing homes, arranging lender help when the buyer raises financing, or agreeing on a later conversation. Be accurate about your role, property status, and what you can promise. Respect the buyer’s decision.
